content: The studies described involve various methodologies and participant groups, with a focus on breastfeeding, child health, and related outcomes. Horta 2006 This study was a prospective cohort study that followed all 5,914 hospital births in Pelotas, Brazil, in 1982, representing over 99% of all deliveries in the region. Detailed information on infant feeding practices was collected prospectively during childhood. Follow-up assessments were conducted in 1997 and 2001, with male participants identified during army recruitment exams in 2000. Blood pressure measurements were taken in 1997 for both sexes, in 2000 for males, and in 2001 for females. The study assessed various risks of bias, including confounding, participant selection, exposure classification, and reporting, all of which were judged to have unclear risk. Iida 2007 This cross-sectional study analyzed data from the 1999–2002 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), which included 1,576 children aged 2 to 5 years. The survey collected information on infant feeding practices, oral health, dietary habits, and family socioeconomic characteristics, typically provided by the child’s primary caregiver, often the mother. Dental examination results were also included. Breastfeeding and its duration (overall, full, and exclusive) were examined using specific criteria, such as whether the child was ever breastfed, the age at which breastfeeding stopped, and the age at which other foods or liquids were introduced. Risks of bias, including confounding, participant selection, and reporting, were judged to have unclear risk. Intusoma 2016 This prospective cohort study analyzed secondary data from a Thai birth cohort in a rural community. The study assessed risks of bias, including selection of reported results, random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding of participants and personnel, all of which were judged to have unclear risk. Izadi 2013 This cross-sectional study used data from the 2009–2010 national survey of school students’ high-risk behaviors in Iran, part of the CASPIAN-III study. The survey included 5,528 students aged 10 to 18 years, recruited through multistage random cluster sampling from urban and rural areas in 27 provinces. Schools were stratified and randomly selected, and students were also chosen randomly. Students with chronic diseases or on medications were excluded. The study collected data on sociodemographic characteristics, birth weight, breastfeeding duration, and other variables. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into five groups: 0 months, less than 6 months, 6–12 months, 12–18 months, and 18–24 months. Outcomes included overweight, obesity, abdominal adiposity, high LDL, high total cholesterol, high triglycerides, high fasting blood sugar, and elevated blood pressure. Risks of bias, including confounding, participant selection, and reporting, were judged to have unclear risk. Jeon 2020 This prospective cohort study utilized data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service (NHIS), which provides health check-up programs for all citizens aged 40 and above and all employees regardless of age. Data were collected for postmenopausal women over 40 who underwent cardiovascular health screenings and breast/cervical cancer screenings between 2009 and 2014. Exclusions included women with prior cancer diagnoses, those diagnosed with cancer within one year of examination, those with prior hysterectomies, those who died within one year of examination, and those with missing data. The primary endpoint was newly diagnosed lung cancer, defined by ICD-10 code C34. The cohort was followed from one year after the health check-up date to the date of lung cancer diagnosis, death, or the end of the study period (December 31, 2016). Risks of bias, including confounding, participant selection, and reporting, were judged to have unclear risk. Karlson 2004 This prospective cohort study followed 121,700 female nurses aged 30–35 years enrolled in the Nurses’ Health Study (NHS) in 1976. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) cases were confirmed through medical record reviews and connective tissue disease screening questionnaires. A total of 674 RA cases were confirmed between 1976 and 2002. For the analysis of breastfeeding and RA risk, 338 patients diagnosed with RA after 1986 (when breastfeeding history was reported) were included. Exclusion criteria included women with RA as of June 1976, those with unconfirmed RA diagnoses, non-responders to supplementary RA questionnaires, and those reporting any cancer (except non-melanomatous skin cancer) at baseline or during follow-up. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as 3 months, 4–11 months, 12–23 months, and 24 or more months. Risks of bias, including confounding, participant selection, and reporting, were judged to have unclear risk. Kersey 2005 This cross-sectional study surveyed children aged 2–5 years in the waiting room of an outpatient clinic at an inner-city community health center in Chicago. The survey included questions about breastfeeding status, such as whether the child was still breastfeeding. Risks of bias, including confounding, participant selection, and reporting, were judged to have unclear risk. Ki 2017 This cross-sectional study analyzed data from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES) 2010–2012, conducted by the Korea Centers for Disease Control. Exclusion criteria included nulliparous women and premenopausal women. Breastfeeding duration per child was calculated by dividing the total breastfeeding period by the number of breastfed children. Participants were divided into four groups: non-breastfeeders, those breastfeeding for 1–6 months per child, 7–12 months per child, 13–18 months per child, and more than 18 months per child. Outcomes included BMI, waist circumference, blood glucose, and lipid profiles. Risks of bias, including confounding, participant selection, and reporting, were judged to have unclear risk. Kikafunda 1998 This cross-sectional study included infants and young children aged 0–30 months from Busimbi subcounty in Mityana county, Mubende district, Central Uganda. Stratified multistage random sampling was used to select households, with 18 villages randomly selected from five parishes. All households with a child under 30 months had an equal chance of participating. A total of 261 children (183 from rural areas and 78 from semi-urban environments) were studied. A comprehensive, precoded questionnaire was validated and piloted before the study. The questionnaires were administered to respondents, preferably the mothers, in their home settings by trained researchers. Risks of bias, including confounding, participant selection, and reporting, were judged to have unclear risk.
